chief_complaint: sudden ischemic stroke in young deep sea diver after surfacing with deep vein thrombosis
hpi_details: 31M scuba diver presenting with acute stroke and DVT where transesophageal echocardiogram with agitated saline bubble study demonstrates right-to-left shunting across a large patent foramen ovale; closure requires multidisciplinary assessment after the acute stroke and venous thrombosis are managed.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Patent Foramen Ovale with Paradoxical Embolism evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Patent Foramen Ovale with Paradoxical Embolism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes completing a full secondary stroke workup to exclude other stroke mechanisms, anticoagulating the confirmed venous thromboembolism, and evaluating percutaneous PFO closure using the RoPE score and shared decision-making once the acute stroke and clot are stabilized, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden ischemic stroke in young deep sea diver after surfacing with deep vein thrombosis

Key HPI features: 31M scuba diver presenting with acute stroke and DVT where transesophageal echocardiogram with agitated saline bubble study demonstrates right-to-left shunting across a large patent foramen ovale; closure requires multidisciplinary assessment after the acute stroke and venous thrombosis are managed.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 84, BP 138/86, afebrile. Neurological exam shows a focal deficit consistent with an embolic infarct in a single arterial territory. Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness, and warmth. MRI brain confirms an acute embolic-pattern infarct. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. Transesophageal echocardiogram with agitated saline bubble study demonstrates a large patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting at rest and with Valsalva. Standard arrhythmia monitoring and carotid/vertebral imaging are unremarkable.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Patent Foramen Ovale with Paradoxical Embolism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Atherosclerotic stroke without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any focal neurological deficit — needs urgent stroke workup regardless of the underlying mechanism.
management_principles: Complete standard secondary stroke workup (arrhythmia monitoring, carotid/vertebral imaging, hypercoagulable workup) to exclude other stroke mechanisms before attributing the stroke to the PFO

Anticoagulate the confirmed deep vein thrombosis per standard duration, then evaluate for percutaneous PFO closure using the RoPE score and shared decision-making once the acute stroke and clot are stabilized
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 31M scuba diver presenting with sudden focal neurological deficit and unilateral leg swelling shortly after surfacing, found to have both acute ischemic stroke and deep vein thrombosis.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 84, BP 138/86, afebrile. Neurological exam shows a focal deficit consistent with an embolic infarct in a single arterial territory. Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness, and warmth. MRI brain confirms an acute embolic-pattern infarct. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. Transesophageal echocardiogram with agitated saline bubble study demonstrates a large patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunting at rest and with Valsalva. Standard arrhythmia monitoring and carotid/vertebral imaging are unremarkable.
reference_soap.assessment: Likely paradoxical embolism through a large patent foramen ovale, with a concurrent lower extremity deep vein thrombosis as the presumed embolic source, after other stroke mechanisms have been excluded.
reference_soap.plan: Complete standard secondary stroke workup (arrhythmia monitoring, carotid/vertebral imaging, hypercoagulable workup) to exclude other stroke mechanisms before attributing the stroke to the PFO. Anticoagulate the confirmed deep vein thrombosis per standard duration, then evaluate for percutaneous PFO closure using the RoPE score and shared decision-making once the acute stroke and clot are stabilized.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical pattern of paradoxical embolism (concurrent stroke and venous thromboembolism in a young patient) that should prompt evaluation for a right-to-left shunt
Formulate a prioritized differential diagnosis for stroke in a young adult, including atherosclerotic stroke, cardioembolic stroke from arrhythmia, and decompression sickness in a diver
Explain the role of the agitated saline bubble study on TEE in demonstrating a PFO and right-to-left shunting
Apply the RoPE score and shared decision-making framework to determine candidacy for percutaneous PFO closure after a cryptogenic stroke

teaching.diagnosis: Patent Foramen Ovale with Paradoxical Embolism
teaching.one_liner: A persistent opening between the heart's atria can allow a venous clot to cross into arterial circulation; a bubble study demonstrates the shunt, while the stroke mechanism and suitability for closure require a full stroke evaluation.
red_flags: Any focal neurological deficit — needs urgent stroke workup regardless of the underlying mechanism

must_ask.say: Were you diving or had you recently surfaced when this started?
What exactly did you notice — weakness, numbness, trouble speaking?
Have you had any leg swelling or pain?
Have you had any long flights or periods of immobility recently?
Do you get migraines, especially with visual auras?

history.answer: About three hours ago, right after I surfaced from a scuba dive, my right arm and right leg suddenly went weak and heavy, and my speech became clumsy.
It is definitely true muscle weakness; my right arm and leg feel heavy, weak, and slightly numb, not just pins and needles.
It is strictly on my right side, affecting my right arm, right leg, and the right corner of my mouth.
It started completely suddenly about three hours ago, right after I got out of the water from my morning dive.
The weakness hit all at once at maximum intensity and has stayed the same since it began.
I cannot grip my dive gear or hold a cup with my right hand, and I have to drag my right foot when trying to walk.
Nothing makes it better or worse; changing positions, moving my neck, or resting does not help at all.
No, I do not have any neck pain, lower back pain, or shooting pains going down my arms or legs.
My speech felt slurred and clumsy, but I have not had any vision loss, double vision, or dizziness.
No, my bowel and bladder habits are completely normal, and I do not have any numbness around my groin or buttocks.
No, I have no shortness of breath, no difficulty chewing or swallowing, and no drooping of my eyelids.
No, I have not noticed any muscle twitching, cramping, or thinning of my arm or leg muscles.
No, I have been feeling completely healthy without any recent colds, fever, or diarrhea.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, but I do not have diabetes or any history of heart rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation.
I eat a normal balanced diet with meat and vegetables, have never had stomach surgery, and drink only occasionally.
I do not take water pills, chemotherapy drugs, or steroids that could affect my muscles or nerves.
No, I do not do repetitive wrist work, lean heavily on my elbows, or spend long hours squatting.
I did a deep-sea dive down to about 30 meters this morning, completed all safety stops, and the weakness started right as I surfaced.
I do not have joint pains, a rash, chest tightness, or breathing problems that would suggest the bends.
My right calf has been swollen, warm, and aching since yesterday, even before I did the dive.
Two days ago I flew on a fourteen-hour nonstop flight to get here, and I stayed seated pretty much the whole trip.
No, I have never had migraines, visual auras, or bad headaches in the past.
I wonder if the diving trip caused a blood clot to travel up to my brain, and I am terrified it could happen again.
I'm terrified that I'll stay paralyzed like this and never be able to dive or work again.
I'm hoping you can give me blood thinners or put me in a dive chamber so I can get full strength back in my arm and leg.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, which were diagnosed about two years ago.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning for my blood pressure, and I do not take any supplements or pain relievers.
I have no known allergies to any medications, latex, or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only drink socially, about one or two beers on weekends, and had no alcohol before the dive.
I work at a desk in digital marketing, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
My father has high blood pressure, but no one in my family has had a stroke, blood clot, or heart attack at a young age.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Right central facial palsy with flattening of the right nasolabial fold and mild dysarthria; extraocular movements and visual fields intact.
Right upper and lower extremity motor strength is 4/5 with right arm pronator drift; normal 5/5 strength on the left without muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the right upper and lower extremities; sensation intact on the left.
Hyperreflexia 3+ at the right biceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons with an extensor Babinski sign on the right; normal 2+ reflexes on the left.
Right-sided dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing due to limb weakness; gait is hemiparetic with right foot dragging.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Right calf shows marked swelling, warmth, and tenderness to palpation, measuring 3 centimeters greater in circumference than the left calf.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory effort and no adventitious sounds.
No midline vertebral spinal tenderness; negative straight-leg raise bilaterally without radicular pain.
